unit: Ch 2: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Overview, Purpose, Status & Scope of the Framework
explain: The Accounting Standards Board (ASB) of ICAI issued the Framework in July 2000 to guide preparation and presentation of financial statements.
It is relevant under Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 notified by the Central Government.
Assists enterprises in preparing statements, ASB in formulating standards, auditors in forming opinions, and users in interpreting reports.
Applies to general-purpose financial statements of commercial, industrial, and business enterprises for external users.
The Framework does not override any specific Accounting Standard; in case of conflict, the Accounting Standard prevails.

flow.title: Role and Authority of Framework
steps: ASB issues Framework in July 2000
Establishes core concepts for financial reports
Guides standard setting and accounting preparation
Assists auditors and external financial users
Accounting Standard overrides Framework during conflict

topics.example: If an Accounting Standard specifies a valuation rule that conflicts with a general Framework concept, the enterprise must follow the Accounting Standard.
remember: Framework issued by ICAI in July 2000.
Specific Accounting Standards ALWAYS override the Framework in case of conflict.
mistakes: Assuming the Framework is a separate Accounting Standard that can override existing standards.

quiz.q: When there is a conflict between an Accounting Standard (AS) and the Framework, which one prevails?
quiz.why: Specific Accounting Standards always override the Framework in case of conflict.

quiz.q: When was the Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements issued by ICAI?
quiz.why: The ASB of ICAI issued the Framework in July 2000.

topics.title: Components of Financial Statements
explain: A complete set of financial statements includes Balance Sheet, Statement of Profit and Loss, Cash Flow Statement, and Notes/Explanatory materials.
Balance Sheet portrays economic resources controlled (assets) and details liquidity and solvency positions.
Statement of Profit and Loss presents operational results and profitability for the accounting period.
Cash Flow Statement shows how an enterprise generates and uses cash across operating, investing, and financing activities.
Notes and supplementary statements disclose accounting policies, segment reporting, earnings per share, and related party transactions.

flow.title: Structure of Complete Financial Statements
steps: Balance Sheet portrays financial position
Profit & Loss depicts operational results
Cash Flow Statement tracks cash activities
Notes disclose accounting policies and details
Interrelated statements deliver a complete view

topics.example: The Balance Sheet shows the total inventory value, while the Notes to Accounts explain the inventory valuation policy used.
remember: A complete set consists of Balance Sheet, P&L, Cash Flow Statement, and Notes with explanatory materials.
mistakes: Treating Cash Flow Statements or Notes as optional attachments rather than mandatory components.

quiz.q: Which component of financial statements reflects an enterprise's liquidity and solvency position?
quiz.why: The Balance Sheet portrays economic resources and provides liquidity and solvency information.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard component of financial statements under the Framework?
quiz.why: Human responsibility reports are outside the standard complete set of financial statements defined by the Framework.

topics.title: Objectives & Users of Financial Statements
explain: The primary objective is providing information about financial position, performance, and cash flows useful for economic decision-making.
Identifies 7 broad user groups: Investors, Employees, Lenders, Suppliers & Creditors, Customers, Government & Agencies, and Public.
Investors assess risk, return, and dividend-paying capacity of their capital.
Employees evaluate employer stability, profitability, remuneration, and job security.
Lenders and Suppliers determine if loans, interest, and credit amounts will be paid on time.
Financial statements suit common user needs but do not contain non-financial information.

flow.title: User Needs Processing Flow
steps: Enterprise prepares general-purpose statements
Reports present position, performance, cash flows
Meets common information needs of users
7 user groups evaluate economic data
Users make informed economic decisions

topics.example: A commercial bank (Lender) analyzes the borrower's Balance Sheet and Cash Flow Statement before approving a term loan.
remember: There are 7 broad user groups of financial statements identified in the Framework.
mistakes: Expecting financial statements to provide detailed non-financial internal management data.

quiz.q: Why are investors primarily interested in financial statements?
o: To assess employer retirement benefit plans
To evaluate investment risk, return, and dividend capacity
To review local supply chain logistics
quiz.why: Investors provide risk capital and need information to evaluate risk, return, and dividend ability.

quiz.q: How many broad groups of users of financial statements are identified by the Framework?
quiz.why: The Framework explicitly identifies 7 broad user groups.

topics.title: Fundamental Accounting Assumptions
explain: Three fundamental assumptions exist: Going Concern, Accrual Basis, and Consistency.
If these assumptions are followed, no explicit disclosure is required in financial statements.
If any fundamental assumption is NOT followed, that specific fact MUST be disclosed.
Going Concern assumes the enterprise will continue operating for the foreseeable future without liquidating or curtailing operations.
Accrual Basis recognizes revenues and costs as earned or incurred, not as cash is received or paid (mandatory under Sec 128(1) Companies Act 2013).
Consistency assumes accounting policies remain unchanged from period to period to ensure comparability.

flow.title: Evaluation of Fundamental Accounting Assumptions
steps: Assume Going Concern, Accrual, and Consistency
Prepare financial statements under assumptions
Check if any assumption was violated
If all followed, no disclosure required
If any violated, disclose fact explicitly

topics.example: If a company plans to liquidate operations next month, it breaches Going Concern and must disclose this fact while valuing assets at Net Realisable Value.
remember: Disclosure is required ONLY when a fundamental accounting assumption is NOT followed.
mistakes: Writing unnecessary notes stating that fundamental assumptions were followed when they are assumed by default.

quiz.q: Under what condition must a fundamental accounting assumption be explicitly disclosed?
o: Only when requested by tax authorities
quiz.why: If fundamental assumptions are followed, no disclosure is required; disclosure is required only if NOT followed.

quiz.q: Which section of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates accrual accounting for companies?
quiz.why: Section 128(1) of Companies Act, 2013 makes accrual accounting mandatory for companies.

topics.title: Qualitative Characteristics of Financial Statements & Constraints
explain: Four principal qualitative characteristics: Understandability, Relevance, Reliability, and Comparability.
Understandability means presentation is clear to users possessing reasonable business knowledge.
Relevance means information influences economic decisions, judged by Materiality (size and nature of item).
Reliability requires data to be free from material error and bias; built on Faithful Representation, Substance Over Form, Neutrality, Prudence, and Completeness.
Comparability requires consistent policy application so users can compare performance across periods and enterprises.
Constraints on relevant and reliable information include Timeliness and Balance between Benefit and Cost.

flow.title: Building Qualitative Financial Information
steps: Present clear data (Understandability)
Include material economic items (Relevance)
Apply prudence, neutrality, completeness (Reliability)
Maintain consistent policies (Comparability)
Balance timeliness with benefit and cost

topics.example: Recording a legal loss provision when probable adheres to Prudence under Reliability, while omitting minor clerical expenses adheres to Materiality under Relevance.
remember: Reliability depends on 5 sub-pillars: Faithful representation, Substance over form, Neutrality, Prudence, and Completeness.
mistakes: Believing more information is always better; dumping irrelevant data creates confusion and violates relevance.

quiz.q: Which qualitative characteristic is evaluated using the concept of Materiality?
quiz.why: Relevance is judged by materiality because misstatement of material items influences economic decisions.

quiz.q: What are the two major constraints on relevant and reliable financial information?
quiz.why: Timeliness and the balance between benefit and cost are the primary constraints mentioned in the Framework.

topics.title: True and Fair View
explain: Financial statements must portray a true and fair view of performance, financial position, and cash flows.
The Framework does not directly define the phrase 'true and fair view'.
Proper application of principal qualitative characteristics and Accounting Standards results in financial statements that present a true and fair view.

flow.title: Path to Achieving True and Fair View
steps: Apply mandatory Accounting Standards
Implement qualitative characteristics systematically
Reflect true economic substance of transactions
Present position and performance accurately
Achieve True and Fair View overall

topics.example: Following AS-1 rules on substance over form ensures that leased assets are recorded accurately to show a true and fair picture.
remember: Compliance with Accounting Standards and qualitative characteristics produces a true and fair view.
mistakes: Treating 'true and fair view' as a standalone mathematical formula instead of an outcome of standard compliance.

quiz.q: How is a true and fair view primarily achieved under the Framework?
o: By applying qualitative characteristics and Accounting Standards
quiz.why: Applying principal qualitative characteristics and appropriate Accounting Standards normally yields a true and fair view.

quiz.q: Does the Framework deal directly with a explicit definition of 'True and Fair View'?
o: No, it does not deal directly with it
quiz.why: The Framework does not deal directly with the concept of true and fair view, but its application leads to it.

topics.title: Elements of Financial Statements & Accounting Relationships
explain: Five elements: Asset, Liability, Equity, Income, and Expense.
Asset: Resource controlled by enterprise from past events, expecting future economic benefit flows.
Liability: Present obligation from past events, expected to result in outflow of resources embodying economic benefits.
Equity: Residual interest in assets after deducting all liabilities (Equity = Assets - Liabilities).
Income: Increase in economic benefits (inflow/enhancement of assets or decrease in liabilities) increasing equity, excluding owner contributions. Includes Revenues and Gains.
Expense: Decrease in economic benefits (outflow/depletion of assets or increase in liabilities) decreasing equity, excluding owner distributions. Includes Expenses and Losses.
Equation: Closing Equity (CE) = Opening Equity (OE) + Capital Introduced (C) + Profit - Drawings (D), where Profit = Income (I) - Expenses (E).

flow.title: Equity and Profit Calculation Flow
steps: Start with Opening Equity (Assets minus Liabilities)
Add fresh Capital Introduced during period
Calculate Profit (Income minus Expenses)
Deduct Drawings or Dividends
Arrive at Closing Equity

topics.example: If a trader settles a ₹31,000 liability by paying ₹30,000 cash, liability decreases by ₹31,000 and asset decreases by ₹30,000, creating ₹1,000 discount income that increases equity.
remember: Gains and Losses are NOT separate elements; gains belong to Income and losses belong to Expenses.
Closing Equity = Opening Equity + Capital Introduced + Profit - Drawings.
mistakes: Classifying provisions for doubtful debts or depreciation as liabilities; they represent asset value diminutions.

quiz.q: Why are Gains and Losses not classified as separate elements of financial statements?
o: Their economic characteristics match Income and Expenses
They only occur in banking companies
They are excluded from the Profit and Loss account
quiz.why: Gains share economic characteristics with Income, and Losses share characteristics with Expenses, so they are not separate elements.

quiz.q: What is the correct relationship for calculating Closing Equity (CE)?
quiz.why: Closing Equity = Opening Equity + Capital Introduced + Profit - Drawings.

topics.title: Measurement of Elements of Financial Statements
explain: Measurement is the process of determining money values at which elements are recognized in financial statements.
Four alternative measurement bases: Historical Cost, Current Cost, Realisable (Settlement) Value, and Present Value.
Historical Cost: Assets recorded at acquisition price (cash paid/fair value); Liabilities at proceeds received or cash expected to pay.
Current Cost: Assets carried at current purchase price of equivalent asset; Liabilities carried at undiscounted amount required to settle currently.
Realisable Value: Assets carried at net selling price on orderly disposal; Liabilities carried at undiscounted settlement amount in normal course.
Present Value: Assets/Liabilities carried at discounted present value of net future cash inflows/outflows.

flow.title: Selecting Measurement Bases
steps: Identify financial statement element
Determine acquisition price (Historical Cost)
Evaluate replacement cost (Current Cost)
Estimate net selling price (Realisable Value)
Calculate discounted cash flows (Present Value)

topics.example: Inventory is initially recorded at Historical Cost upon acquisition, but at year-end it is valued at lower of cost and net realisable value.
remember: Historical Cost is the standard base primarily used, but other bases are applied in combinations as per Accounting Standards.
mistakes: Assuming Current Cost liabilities are discounted; under Current Cost, liabilities are stated at undiscounted amounts.

quiz.q: Which measurement basis carries assets at the cash amount that would have to be paid if the same asset was acquired currently?
quiz.why: Current Cost carries assets at the cash equivalent required to acquire an equivalent asset currently.

quiz.q: How are liabilities measured under the Present Value convention?
o: At present value of future net cash outflows
At lower of cost and net realisable value
quiz.why: Under Present Value, liabilities are carried at the discounted present value of future net cash outflows required to settle them.

topics.title: Concepts of Capital Maintenance & Profit Determination
explain: Capital refers to net assets (CA - CL). Capital maintenance ensures net assets are preserved to maintain operational capacity.
Retained Profit = Closing Equity - Capital to be maintained. A positive retained profit ensures capital maintenance.
Financial Capital Maintenance at Historical Cost: Assets stated at historical costs. Capital maintained if retained profit >= 0. Ignores price inflation.
Financial Capital Maintenance at Current Purchasing Power (CPP): Opening equity restated using general average price index.
Physical Capital Maintenance at Current Costs: Opening assets restated using specific price indices applicable to each asset, ensuring physical productive capacity is preserved.

flow.title: Capital Maintenance Calculation Process
steps: Determine Opening Equity and Closing Equity
Select maintenance basis (Historical, CPP, or Physical)
Restate Opening Capital using applicable price index
Deduct Restated Capital from Closing Equity
Check if Retained Profit is positive or negative

topics.example: A trader starts with ₹12,000 (6,000 units @ ₹2). If closing unit price rises to ₹2.50, physical capital required is ₹15,000 (6,000 x ₹2.50). If closing cash is ₹12,000 after ₹6,000 drawings, retained profit is (-) ₹3,000, failing physical capital maintenance.
remember: CPP uses general average price indices, whereas Physical Capital Maintenance uses specific price indices.
mistakes: Confusing general price indices (CPP method) with specific price indices (Physical capital maintenance method).

quiz.q: Which capital maintenance concept restates opening capital using specific price indices of assets?
o: Financial Capital Maintenance at Historical Cost
Financial Capital Maintenance at Current Purchasing Power
Physical Capital Maintenance at Current Costs
quiz.why: Physical capital maintenance uses specific price indices for each asset to preserve physical operating capacity.

quiz.q: Under Financial Capital Maintenance at Current Purchasing Power (CPP), what index restates opening equity?
o: Wholesale price index of raw materials
quiz.why: CPP restates historical equity using general average price indices.
